cases.description: Microsoft's documented example string: byte length of an 11-character ASCII string
cases.expected_note: Microsoft's LEN/LENB page uses 'Phoenix, AZ' as its worked example and publishes LEN = 11. The DBCS rule (see the LENB_non_ascii_characters case) cannot change the answer here because every character is single-byte under either reading. NOTE: the current live page now states 'The LENB function is deprecated' and has dropped the DBCS explanation entirely

cases.description: An empty string has zero bytes
cases.expected_note: No characters means no bytes, under either the DBCS or the non-DBCS rule

cases.description: Spaces are characters and are counted, including leading and trailing ones
cases.expected_note: Microsoft documents 'Spaces count as characters' for the text argument of LEN/LENB; the string here is two spaces, three letters and three spaces = 8

cases.description: A numeric argument is converted to its text representation before measuring
cases.expected_note: The number 1234 becomes the four-character string "1234", so the byte length is 4 in a non-DBCS default language

cases.description: DIVERGENCE PROBE: two CJK characters, where the byte count depends on the DBCS language rule
cases.expected_note: Verbatim from Microsoft's archived LEN/LENB page: 'LENB counts 2 bytes per character only when a DBCS language is set as the default language. Otherwise LENB behaves the same as LEN, counting 1 byte per character', with DBCS listed as Japanese, Chinese (Simplified/Traditional) and Korean. The harness runs under a non-DBCS default locale, so the documented answer is 2 (LEN semantics). An engine that always counts raw UTF-8 or UTF-16 bytes returns 6 or 4 instead -- recording which one each engine does is the point of this case

cases.description: An error argument propagates instead of being measured
cases.expected_note: The argument evaluates to #DIV/0! before LENB sees it, so the error is the result
